en: The Parivāra:
The Analysis of the Monastic Rules (Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga), First Part
1.2 Section on the Occurrence of Offenses 1.
Chapter on Defeat (Pārājika):
While engaging in sexual intercourse, how many offenses does one incur?
One who engages in sexual intercourse incurs three offenses:
if one engages in sexual intercourse with a body that is not mostly consumed by fire, it is an offense of defeat (pārājika);
if one engages in sexual intercourse with a body that is mostly consumed by fire, it is a serious offense (thullaccaya).
If he inserts the penis without touching it into a mouth that has been turned upward, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
While engaging in sexual intercourse, one incurs these three offenses.
When taking what is not given, how many offenses does one incur?
One who takes what is not given incurs three offenses.
If one takes what is not given, valued at five māsakas or more than five māsakas, by way of theft, it is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
If one takes what is not given, valued at more than one māsaka but less than five māsakas, by way of theft, it is a grave offense (thullaccaya).
If one takes what has not been given, by way of theft, to the value of a māsaka or less than a māsaka, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
While taking what has not been given, one incurs these three offenses.
How many offenses does one incur when intentionally depriving a human being of life?
One who intentionally deprives a human being of life incurs three offenses.
If one digs a pit aiming at a human being with the thought, "May he fall in and die," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
when the person falls and painful feeling arises, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
If he kills, there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).
One who intentionally deprives a human being of life incurs these three offenses.
How many offenses does one incur when claiming a non-existent, unreal superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*)?
One who falsely claims a non-existent, unactualized superhuman state incurs three offenses.
If one with evil desires, driven by longing, falsely claims a non-existent, unactualized superhuman state, it is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).
If he says, "The monk who dwells in your monastery is an arahant," it is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya) for the listener who understands him.
For one who does not recognize [the truth], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
By falsely claiming a non-existent, unreal superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma), one incurs these three offenses.
The four rules on defeat (pārājika) are concluded.
2. Saṅghādisesa Section (…) One who, having made an effort, emits semen, incurs three offenses:
if he intends, makes an effort, and emission occurs, it is a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
If he intends and makes an effort, but does not emit, there is a thullaccaya offense;
for the preliminary action, there is a dukkaṭa offense.
One who engages in physical contact with a woman incurs three offenses.
If one touches body with body, it is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa);
if one touches what is connected to the body with the body, it is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya);
if one touches what is connected to the body with what is connected to the body, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
One who addresses a woman with lewd words incurs three offenses.
If, referring to the anus or the urinary tract, one speaks in praise or speaks in dispraise, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
Excluding the anus and the urinary tract, if one refers to the area below the collarbone and above the knees, speaking in praise or speaking in dispraise, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya).
If, referring to something connected with the body, one speaks in praise or speaks in dispraise, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
One who speaks in praise of serving one’s own lustful desires incurs three offenses:
if he speaks in praise of serving one’s own lustful desires in the presence of a woman, there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
If one speaks in praise of serving one’s own sensual desires in the presence of a paṇḍaka, there is an offense of thullaccaya;
if one speaks in praise of serving one’s own sensual desires in the presence of an animal, there is an offense of dukkaṭa.
One who engages in matchmaking incurs three offenses.
If she accepts it, examines it, and brings it back, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa);
if she accepts it and examines it but does not bring it back, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya);
if she accepts it but does not examine it and does not bring it back, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
One who has a hut built by means of a formal request incurs three offenses:
for the act of having it built, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) regarding the preliminary effort;
when one bundle of materials remains unarrived, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
When that lump has arrived, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
One who causes a large dwelling to be built incurs three offenses:
for the act of causing it to be built, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and so forth].
If a morsel has not yet arrived, there is an offense of thullaccaya;
when that morsel arrives, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
One who groundlessly charges a bhikkhu with an offense entailing defeat (pārājika) incurs three offenses.
If, having caused [the monk] to grant leave, he speaks with the intention of causing him to fall away, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa* and *dukkaṭa*.
If, having caused [the monk] to grant leave, he speaks with the intention of reviling him, there is an offense of abusive speech (*omasavāda*).

By charging a bhikkhu with an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*) on account of some minor point or pretext from a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) pertaining to something else, one incurs three offenses.
If one speaks with the intention of causing [the monk] to leave after having had him grant leave, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa* and an offense of *dukkaṭa*;
if one speaks with the intention of reviling after having had him grant leave, there is an offense of abusive speech (*omasavāda*).
A monk who causes a schism in the Saṅgha and does not desist even after being admonished up to three times incurs three offenses.
For the motion, there is an offense of wrong-doing;
for two proclamations, there are offenses of serious transgression;
at the conclusion of the proclamation, there is an offense entailing suspension from the Saṅgha.
Monks who follow those who cause schism, by not desisting even after being exhorted up to three times, incur three offenses:
on the motion, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
with the two proclamations, offenses of grave wrongdoing (thullaccaya).
At the conclusion of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
A monk who is difficult to speak with, not relinquishing [his position] despite being exhorted up to three times, incurs three offenses:
for the motion (*ñatti*), there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);...
With two proclamations, there are thullaccaya offenses;
at the conclusion of the proclamation, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
A monk who corrupts families, failing to desist after being formally admonished up to three times, incurs three offenses.
For the motion, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for two proclamations, there are offenses of serious transgression (thullaccaya);
at the conclusion of the proclamation, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
The thirteen Saṅghādisesas are finished.
4. The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa) 4.1. The Chapter on the Kathina (Kathinavagga)
One incurs one offense by keeping an extra robe beyond ten days:
a *nissaggiya-pācittiya*.
One incurs one offense by staying apart from one’s three robes for even a single night.
It is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
Having accepted an out-of-season robe, if one lets a month pass, one commits one offense:
it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If one has an unrelated nun wash an old robe, one incurs two offenses:
for the act of having her wash it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
once it has been washed, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya pācittiya*).
One who accepts a robe from the hand of an unrelated nun incurs two offenses:
for the act of taking, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once it is taken, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
When requesting a robe from an unrelated householder or housewife, one incurs two offenses:
for the act of requesting, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
once it has been requested, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
If one requests more than that amount of robe-cloth from an unrelated householder or housewife, one incurs two offenses:
for the act of requesting, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once it has been requested, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If one approaches an unrelated householder who has not previously invited one and makes a request regarding a robe, one incurs two offenses:
for the act of making the request, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
when the request has been made, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya pācittiya*).
If, without having been previously invited, one approaches unrelated householders and makes a request regarding a robe, one incurs two offenses:
for the act of making the request, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
once the request has been made, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya pācittiya*).
If one procures a robe by urging more than three times or by standing more than six times, one incurs two offenses:
for the effort, a dukkaṭa;
when it has been procured, a nissaggiya pācittiya.
The First Chapter on the Kathina.
4.2. The Chapter on Silk.
One who has a blanket made mixed with silk incurs two offenses.

If he causes it to be made, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of preparation; once it has been caused to be made, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
One who causes a rug to be made from pure black wool incurs two offenses.
If he causes it to be made, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of preparation; once it has been caused to be made, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If he causes a new rug to be made without taking one measure of white wool and one measure of brown wool, he incurs two offenses.

If he causes it to be made, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of preparation; once it has been caused to be made, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
One who causes a sitting mat to be made every year incurs two offenses.
If he causes it to be made, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the effort;
once it has been caused to be made, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If, without leaving a border of one Sugata-span around the old sitting rug, he causes a new sitting rug to be made, he incurs two offenses.
If he causes it to be made, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the effort;
when it has been made, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
Having accepted sheep’s wool, one incurs two offenses while traveling more than three yojanas.
If he causes the first foot to pass three *yojanas*, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
if he causes the second foot to pass, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
In having an unrelated nun wash woolen fleece, one incurs two offenses.
If he causes it to be washed, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the attempt;
once it has been caused to be washed, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
One who accepts money incurs two offenses.
He takes it: for the effort, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once it is taken, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
One who engages in various kinds of transactions involving money incurs two offenses.
One enters [into the transaction]; for the effort, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
when one has entered, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
One who engages in various kinds of buying and selling incurs two offenses.

He enters [the state of meditation]: for the effort, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); when he has entered it, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The second section on silk is finished.
4.3. The Section on Alms Bowls (Pattavagga) One incurs one offense by keeping an extra alms bowl for more than ten days:
a *nissaggiya pācittiya*.
When one exchanges an almsbowl that has fewer than five mends for another new bowl, one incurs two offenses:
for the act of exchanging, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
once it has been exchanged, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya pācittiya*).
Having accepted medicines, one incurs one offense by keeping them beyond seven days:
a *nissaggiya pācittiya*.
While the summer season has more than a month remaining, one incurs two offenses while seeking a rain-season robe (*vassikasāṭikacīvara*).
If he searches for it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
when it has been searched for, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
Having personally given a robe to a bhikkhu, if he takes it back while angry and displeased, he incurs two offenses.
In the act of taking it away, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once it has been taken away, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
By personally requesting thread and then having weavers weave a robe, one incurs two offenses.
When he causes it to be woven, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the effort;
when it has been woven, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
If, without having been previously invited, he approaches a weaver who is not related to him as a householder and makes a specification regarding the robe, he incurs two offenses.
If he makes a formal resolution, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act;
once the resolution has been made, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
Having accepted a robe that is urgently needed, if he lets the robe-season pass by, he incurs one offense.
An offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
Having deposited any one of the three robes within an inhabited area, one commits one offense by staying apart from it for more than four nights:
an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
One who, knowing that a gain intended for the Saṅgha has been dedicated, dedicates it to oneself, incurs two offenses:
for the act of dedicating it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once it has been dedicated, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Third Chapter on Robes.
The thirty offenses entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya) are concluded.
5. The Section on Offenses Entailing Confession (Pācittiyakaṇḍa).
5.1. The Chapter on False Speech (Musāvādavagga).
How many offenses does one incur by speaking a deliberate lie?
One who speaks a deliberate lie incurs five offenses.
If one who is of evil desire and overcome by desire speaks of a non-existent, unreal superhuman state, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
If one groundlessly accuses a monk of an offense entailing defeat, there is an offense of formal meeting (saṅghādisesa).
If one says, "The monk who dwells in your monastery is an arahant," there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya) for one who understands [the meaning].
For one who does not understand, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for a deliberate lie, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
While speaking a deliberate lie, one incurs these five offenses.
By insulting, one incurs two offenses:
if one insults one who is fully ordained, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya);
if one insults one who is not fully ordained, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
One who engages in malicious talebearing incurs two offenses:
if one engages in malicious talebearing against one who is fully ordained, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya);
if one engages in malicious talebearing against one who is not fully ordained, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
One who teaches the Dhamma word by word to one who is not fully ordained incurs two offenses:
for the act of teaching, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every word, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who, being unordained, shares a sleeping place for more than two or three nights incurs two offenses:
for the act of lying down, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once he has lain down, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who shares a sleeping place with a woman incurs two offenses:
while lying down, there is an offense of wrong conduct (*dukkaṭa*) for the act of undertaking;
once she has lain down, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
One who teaches the Dhamma to a woman with more than five or six words incurs two offenses:
for the act of teaching, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every word [beyond that], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who reports a real superhuman state to one who is not fully ordained incurs two offenses:
for the act of reporting, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once reported, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
When a monk reports a grave offense of another monk to one who is not fully ordained, he incurs two offenses:
for the act of reporting, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once reported, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
While digging the earth, one incurs two offenses:
for the act of digging, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every stroke, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The First Chapter on False Speech.
5.2. The Chapter on Vegetation.
One incurs two offenses by destroying vegetation.
In the act of causing it to fall, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every blow, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
While evading one thing with another, he incurs two offenses.
If one evades by speaking about something else when evasion has not been formally charged, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
if one evades by speaking about something else when evasion has been formally charged, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
By censuring a bhikkhu, one incurs two offenses.
If she causes [the Sangha] to be criticized, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the attempt;
once it has been criticized, there is an offense entailing expiation.
Having spread out a bed, a bench, a mattress, or a rug belonging to the Sangha in the open air, if she departs without putting them away and without asking permission, she incurs two offenses.
If he steps over the first throw of a clod, there is an offense of wrong-doing;
if he steps over the second foot, there is an offense entailing expiation.
Having spread out a bed in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, if he departs without putting it away and without informing anyone, he incurs two offenses.
If he steps across the enclosure with the first foot, there is an offense of wrong-doing;
if he steps across with the second foot, there is an offense entailing expiation.
In a dwelling belonging to the Sangha, if he knowingly makes his bed intruding upon a monk who has already arrived, he incurs two offenses.
If he lies down, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the effort;
when he has lain down, there is an offense entailing expiation.
A monk, being angry and displeased, while ejecting another from a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, incurs two offenses.
In the act of throwing out, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once thrown out, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
When one sits down on a bed or a bench with detachable legs in an upper-story room of a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, one incurs two offenses.
He sits down: there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the act of preparation;
once he has sat down, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
If, having resolved [to sit] two or three times, he resolves more than that, he incurs two offenses.
When one resolves [to use it], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) regarding the preparation;
once resolved, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who knowingly sprinkles water containing living beings onto grass or clay incurs two offenses.
If he sprinkles [water], there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act;
when it has been sprinkled, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
The second section on plants.
5.3. Ovādavagga:
One who instructs the bhikkhunīs without being authorized incurs two offenses.
While in the process of instructing, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he exhorts them when it has not yet set, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

If he exhorts the bhikkhunīs after the sun has set, he incurs two offenses: for the act of exhorting, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and for the completion of the exhortation, an offense of expiation].
If he exhorts them, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

By approaching the nuns’ quarters and exhorting the nuns, he incurs two offenses: for the act of exhorting, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and for the exhortation itself, an offense of expiation].
If he has exhorted them, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
By saying, “The monks are exhorting the nuns for the sake of material gain,” one incurs two offenses:
for the act of speaking, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [and for the completion of the statement, an offense of expiation].
When it has been spoken, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
One who gives a robe to an unrelated nun incurs two offenses:
for the act of giving, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); [and upon completion, the *pācittiya*].
If she has given it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

While sewing a robe for an unrelated nun, one incurs two offenses: for the act of sewing, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and when the robe is finished, an offense of expiation].
At every arrow-shot, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who sets out on a journey along a road together with a bhikkhunī, having made an appointment, incurs two offenses:
for the act of setting out, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [and for each arrow-shot thereafter, an offense of expiation].
If he embarks upon it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
By making an appointment with a bhikkhunī and boarding the same boat, one incurs two offenses:
for the act of boarding, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [and for the completion of the act, an offense of expiation].
If he has climbed up, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who knowingly eats almsfood prepared by a nun incurs two offenses:
when he accepts it with the thought, "I will eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [when he eats it, there is an offense of expiation].
For every mouthful, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who arranges a private sitting with a bhikkhunī, alone with one alone, incurs two offenses:
for the act of sitting down, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [for the completion of the act, an offense of expiation].
If she sits [with him], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The third section, on Exhortation, is concluded.
5.4. The Section on Food.
If one eats an alms-meal at a lodging more than once, one incurs two offenses:
when one receives it with the intention, "I will eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who eats a meal in a group incurs two offenses:
if one receives [the food] with the intention, "I will eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
While eating in succession, one incurs two offenses:
if one accepts [the food] thinking, "I will eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Having accepted two or three bowlfuls of fried cakes, if he accepts more than that, he incurs two offenses:
for the act of taking, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once they have been taken, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who, having finished eating and being invited to stop, eats fresh or cooked food that is not left over, incurs two offenses:
if he accepts it with the intention, "I will eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one invites a monk who has already finished his meal and refused further food by offering him fresh or soft food that is not left over, one incurs two offenses.
By accepting it with the words, "I will eat it, I will consume it," at his request, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
at the conclusion of the meal, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who eats solid food or soft food at an improper time incurs two offenses:
if he receives it with the intention, "I will eat it," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
While eating stored-up fresh or cooked food, one incurs two offenses:
if one receives it with the intention, "I will eat it," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who, for one's own sake, requests and eats exquisite foods, incurs two offenses:
when one accepts them with the thought, "I shall eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who takes food that has not been given through the gateway of the mouth incurs two offenses:
if one receives it with the thought, "I shall eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every swallow, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The fourth chapter on Food is finished.
5.5. The Chapter on the Naked Ascetics:
One incurs two offenses by personally giving fresh or cooked food to a naked ascetic (acelaka), a male wanderer (paribbājaka), or a female wanderer (paribbājikā).
In the act of giving, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once it has been given, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
If he dismisses a bhikkhu by saying, “Come, friend, let us enter a village or town for alms,” whether he causes food to be given to him or does not cause it to be given, he incurs two offenses.
In the act of urging [her to leave], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once she has been urged, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
By forcing oneself into a family where food is being served and sitting down, one incurs two offenses.
He sits down: there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the act of preparation;
once he has sat down, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
One who arranges to sit in secret on a concealed seat together with a woman incurs two offenses.
He sits down: for the effort, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once seated, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
One who arranges to sit alone with a woman in private incurs two offenses.
As he sits down, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the act;
once seated, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Being invited and having already finished his meal, one who goes on a visit to families either before the meal or after the meal incurs two offenses.
When he steps over the threshold with the first foot, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
when he steps over it with the second foot, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
By requesting medicine beyond that amount, one incurs two offenses.
If she requests it, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of requesting;
once requested, there is an offense entailing expiation.
One who goes to see an army on campaign incurs two offenses.
If he goes, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
if he stands where he sees [the army], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
While staying with the army for more than three nights, he incurs two offenses.
While making preparations to stay, there is an offense of wrong-doing;
when he has stayed, there is an offense entailing expiation.
One who goes to a military spectacle incurs two offenses.
If he goes, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
if he sees it while standing where he is, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The fifth section, on the naked ascetics (acelaka), is concluded.
5.6. Surāmerayavagga:
One who drinks fermented liquor (majja) incurs two offenses.
If one accepts it with the intention, "I shall drink," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For every mouthful, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

By tickling a bhikkhu with his fingers to make him laugh, he incurs two offenses: for the act of making him laugh, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and for the laughter itself, an offense of expiation].
In laughing, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
While playing in water, one incurs two offenses:
if one plays in water that reaches below the ankle, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [if it reaches above the ankle, there is an offense of expiation].
If he plays at the tops of his ankles, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who acts with disrespect incurs two offenses: for the preliminary effort, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [for the completion of the act, there is an offense of expiation].
When it is finished, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who frightens a bhikkhu incurs two offenses:
for the act of frightening, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and an offense of expiation upon completion].
If one causes [another] to be frightened, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Having kindled a fire, if one warms oneself, one incurs two offenses:
for the act of kindling it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [and for warming oneself, there is an offense of expiation].
If she bathes within half a month, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who bathes within half a month incurs two offenses:
for the act of bathing, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and the full offense upon completion].
At the conclusion of bathing, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
If one uses a new robe without applying any one of the three methods for disfiguring it, one incurs two offenses:
for the act of using it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and upon completion, the offense of expiation].
If he uses it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

By using a robe that has been assigned to himself by a monk, a nun, a female trainee (sikkhamānā), a male novice (sāmaṇera), or a female novice (sāmaṇerī), without having had the assignment formally relinquished, one incurs two offenses:
for the act of using it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and for the actual use, an offense of expiation].
If he uses [it], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
When a monk is removing another monk’s bowl, robe, sitting mat, needle case, or waistband, he incurs two offenses:
for the act of removing it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [and upon its removal, an offense of expiation].
If one drinks [it] intentionally, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The sixth section: On Intoxicants. 5.7.
The Section on Water Containing Living Beings.
When intentionally depriving a living being of life, how many offenses does one incur?
When intentionally depriving a living being of life, one incurs four offenses.
If one digs a pit without specifying [the victim], thinking, “Whoever falls in will die,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If a human falls into it and dies, there is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika);
if a yakkha, a peta, or one who is an animal in human form falls into it and dies, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya);
if an animal falls into it and dies, there is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
One who intentionally deprives a living being of life incurs these four offenses.
One who knowingly consumes water containing living beings incurs two offenses:
for the act of consuming, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); [and for the actual consumption, a *pācittiya*].
If he makes use of it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who, knowing that a legal issue has been settled according to the Dhamma, reopens it for a further formal act, incurs two offenses:
for the act of reopening, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and for the actual reopening, an offense of expiation].
If one opens [a settled legal question], there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
A bhikkhu who knowingly conceals a grave offense commits one offense, an offense entailing expiation.
One who knowingly confers full ordination on a person less than twenty years of age commits two offenses.
If one ordains [another], there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of preparation;
once ordained, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who knowingly travels along a highway in company with a band of thieves in concert commits two offenses.
If he sets out, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of preparation;
when he has set out, there is an offense entailing expiation.
One who sets out on a journey together with a woman after making an appointment incurs two offenses.
If he proceeds with the effort, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once he has proceeded, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
One who does not relinquish a wicked view after being exhorted up to three times incurs two offenses.
By the motion, there is an offense of wrong-doing;
at the conclusion of the formal act, there is an offense entailing expiation.
By associating with a monk who speaks thus knowingly, who has not acted in accordance with the Dhamma, and who has not relinquished that view, one incurs two offenses.
While preparing to eat together, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once the meal has been eaten together, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
One who, knowing that a novice (samaṇuddesa) has been thus expelled, supports him, incurs two offenses.
If she entices [him], there is an offense of wrong-doing for the preliminary effort;
when he has been enticed, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The seventh section, on [food] containing living beings, is concluded.
5.8. The Section on Legitimate Matters (Sahadhammikavagga).

When being told something legitimate by fellow monks, if one says, “Friends, I will not train in this training rule until I have consulted another monk who is competent and an expert in the Vinaya,” one incurs two offenses.
For the mere act of saying it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort.
When it has been spoken, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
One who disparages the Vinaya incurs two offenses:
for the act of disparaging, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the preliminary effort; [and when it is completed, an offense of expiation].
If she disparages [him], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
While causing confusion, she incurs two offenses:

if she causes confusion regarding what has not been charged as confusion, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [if she causes confusion regarding what has been so charged, there is an offense of expiation].
If one causes delusion in one who is already deluded, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
When a monk, being angry and displeased, gives a blow, he incurs two offenses:
for the preliminary effort, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [for the actual blow, there is an offense of expiation].
If he strikes him, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
When a monk, angry and displeased, brandishes his hand like a palm-leaf fan, he incurs two offenses:
for the act of brandishing it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); [and for striking, an offense of expiation].
When it has been exhaled, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who groundlessly charges a bhikkhu with a saṅghādisesa offense incurs two offenses:
for the act of charging, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and when the charge is made, an offense of expiation].
If he does not scold him, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who intentionally causes a bhikkhu to feel remorse incurs two offenses:
for the act of causing it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and an offense of expiation upon completion].
If it is placed [on the fire], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Standing eavesdropping on monks who have fallen into quarreling, brawling, and disputes, one incurs two offenses:
if one goes [to listen] thinking, "I shall hear," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [if one hears anything, there is an offense of expiation].
Wherever one stands while listening, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Having given consent for formal acts that are in accordance with the Dhamma, one who subsequently falls into the practice of criticizing them incurs two offenses:
for the act of criticizing, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and an offense of expiation when the criticism is completed].
If one speaks disparagingly, one incurs an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
When a formal discussion of a legal matter is underway in the Saṅgha, by rising from one's seat and departing without having given one's consent, one incurs two offenses:
for leaving the reach of the assembly's hand, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [and for departing, there is an offense entailing expiation].
If he departs, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
Having given a robe by a unanimous Saṅgha, one who subsequently falls into the practice of criticizing incurs two offenses:
for the act of criticizing, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort; [and the full offense upon completion].
If one misappropriates it, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
One who, knowing that a gain intended for the Saṅgha has been dedicated to an individual, dedicates it to that individual, incurs two offenses:
for the act of dedicating it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [and upon its completion, an offense entailing expiation].
If it is diverted [for another purpose], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The eighth section, on those of the same Dhamma.
5.9. The Section on Kings.
Entering the royal palace without prior announcement, one incurs two offenses:
when one crosses the threshold with the first foot, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
when one crosses with the second foot, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who acquires a jewel incurs two offenses:
for the act of taking it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once it is acquired, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If a bhikkhu enters a village at an improper time without having asked permission from a bhikkhu who is present, he incurs two offenses:
when he steps over the first threshold, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
when he steps over the second threshold, he commits an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
One who has a needle case made of bone, ivory, or horn incurs two offenses:
for the act of having it made, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once it has been made, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who has a bed or a chair made that exceeds the proper measure incurs two offenses:
for the act of having it made, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once it has been made, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who has a bed or a chair made covered with cotton commits two offenses:
while making it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the act of undertaking;
once it is made, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who has a sitting mat made exceeding the proper measure incurs two offenses:
for the act of having it made, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once it has been made, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who has a itch-covering cloth made that exceeds the proper measure incurs two offenses:
for the act of having it made, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once it is made, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
One who has a rain-cloak made exceeding the proper measure incurs two offenses:
for the act of having it made, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
once it has been made, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
When one has a robe made to the measure of a Sugata’s robe, how many offenses does one incur?

When having a robe made to the measure of a Sugata’s robe, one incurs two offenses: while in the process of having it made, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); [and when it is finished, a *nissaggiya pācittiya*].
When having [a robe] made, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)—
one who has a robe made to the measure of the Sugata’s robe incurs these two offenses.
This is the ninth section, the Chapter on Kings.
The Minor Rules (Khuddaka) are finished.
6. The Section on Confession (Pāṭidesanīyakaṇḍa).
How many offenses does one commit by eating fresh or cooked food after having personally received it from the hand of an unrelated bhikkhunī who has entered among the houses?
If he receives fresh or cooked food directly from the hand of an unrelated bhikkhunī who has entered an inhabited area and eats it, he commits two offenses:
when he receives it with the intention, "I will eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful he swallows, there is an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
If one receives fresh or cooked food directly from the hand of an unrelated nun who has entered among the houses and eats it, one incurs two offenses.
If one eats while a nun is giving directions and does not stop her, one incurs two offenses:
if one accepts [the food] thinking, "I will eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [and when eating, there is an offense of expiation].
For every mouthful, there is an offense entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*).
When eating either fresh or cooked food after having received it with one's own hand from families designated as "those in training," one incurs two offenses:
by receiving it with the thought, "I shall eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); [and for each mouthful, an offense entailing confession].
For every mouthful, there is an offense entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*).
When one eats fresh or cooked food that has not been previously announced in forest lodgings, having received it with one's own hand within the monastery grounds, how many offenses does one incur?
One who eats fresh or cooked food that has not been previously announced in forest lodgings, having received it with one's own hand within the monastery grounds, incurs two offenses.
If one accepts [food] thinking, "I will eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
One who, in forest dwellings, having previously received no invitation, accepts fresh or cooked food with his own hand within the monastery and eats it, incurs these two offenses.
The four rules on offenses entailing acknowledgment are finished.
7. The Section on Training Rules 7.1.
The Chapter on Being All Around.
In dependence on disrespect, how many offenses does one commit when wearing the lower robe hanging down in front or behind?
In dependence on disrespect, while wearing the lower robe hanging down in front or behind, one commits one offense:
an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, one commits this one offense by wearing the lower robe hanging down either in front or behind.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by putting on the upper robe hanging down either in front or behind;
it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by walking through an inhabited area with the body uncovered:
an *dukkaṭa*.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by sitting down in an inhabited area with the body uncovered: an *dukkaṭa*.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, while walking through an inhabited area, one commits one offense by playing with one's hand or foot:
an offense of wrong-doing.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by playing with one’s hands or feet while sitting inside a house:
an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by looking here and there while walking inside a house.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
By looking here and there while sitting within an inhabited area out of disrespect, one commits one offense:
an offense of wrong-doing.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by walking with the body lifted up in an inhabited area:
an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by sitting with the body lifted up in an inhabited area: an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
The first chapter, on the circular [robe], is finished.
7.2. The Chapter on Excessive Laughter (ujjagghika-vagga).
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by laughing loudly while walking in an inhabited area:
an *dukkaṭa*.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by sitting with loud laughter in an inhabited area: an *dukkaṭa*.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, while walking through an inhabited area making loud noises and a great clamor, one commits one offense:
an offense of wrong-doing.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by sitting in a house with loud voices and making a great noise:
an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by swaying the body while walking in a house: an offense of wrong-doing.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
By sitting with the body swaying in an inhabited area out of disrespect, one commits one offense:
an offense of wrong-doing.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by swinging one’s arms while walking in an inhabited area:
an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by swinging one’s arms while sitting in an inhabited area: an offense of wrong-doing.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
By walking with the head shaking in an inhabited area out of disrespect, one incurs one offense:
an offense of wrong-doing.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by nodding the head while sitting in an inhabited area:
an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
This is the second section on laughing loudly.
7.3. Khambhakata-vagga:
Regarding lack of respect, one who walks with hands on hips in an inhabited area incurs one offense:
an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by sitting with hands on the hips in an inhabited area:
an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by walking with the head covered in an inhabited area: an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, one who sits with his head covered while in an inhabited area incurs one offense:
an offense of wrong-doing.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by walking on tiptoe in an inhabited area:
an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by sitting with legs crossed in an inhabited area.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
By receiving almsfood disrespectfully out of a lack of reverence, one incurs one offense:
an offense of wrong-doing.
Out of disrespect, while receiving almsfood while looking here and there, one commits one offense:
an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, while receiving an excessive amount of curry alone, one commits one offense.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
One who, out of disrespect, receives almsfood piled up in a heap commits one offense:
an offense of wrong-doing.
The third chapter, on Standing.
7.4. The Chapter on Almsfood:
One commits one offense by eating almsfood without due care, out of disrespect.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, while eating almsfood while looking here and there, one commits one offense:
an offense of wrong-doing.
Out of disrespect, while eating almsfood after picking it up here and there, one commits one offense:
an *dukkaṭa*.
Out of disrespect, while eating too much curry, one commits one offense: an *dukkaṭa*.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
By reason of disrespect, one who eats almsfood after having crushed it from a heap commits one offense:
an offense of wrong-doing.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by covering curry or sauce with rice:
an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by having curry or rice requested for one’s own sake and eating it when not ill.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, perceiving it as a fault while looking at the alms-bowl of others, one incurs one offense:
an offense of wrong-doing.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by making a mouthful too large:
an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by making a mouthful too long.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
The fourth chapter on almsfood (piṇḍapāta) is concluded. 7.5.
The Chapter on Mouthfuls (kabaḷa).
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by opening the mouth while a morsel has not yet been brought to it:
an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by thrusting the entire hand into the mouth while eating.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
By speaking with food still in one’s mouth out of disrespect, one commits one offense:
an offense of wrong-doing.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by eating while tossing up morsels of food:
an *dukkaṭa*.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by eating while breaking up morsels of food: an *dukkaṭa*.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
By eating with a lump in one's cheek out of disrespect, one commits one offense:
an offense of wrong-doing.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by shaking one's hand while eating:
an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by scattering rice grains while eating.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
One who, out of disrespect, eats while sticking out the tongue, incurs one offense:
an offense of wrong-doing.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by making a *capucapu* sound while eating.
It is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
The fifth section on mouthfuls is concluded.
7.6. The Section on Making a Surusuru Sound.
One who eats making a *surusuru* sound out of disrespect commits one offense:
an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by licking one’s hand while eating:
an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by licking one’s bowl while eating: an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
By eating while licking the lips out of disrespect, one commits one offense:
an offense of wrong-doing.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by receiving a water vessel with a hand that has food on it:
an *dukkaṭa*.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by discarding bowl-washing water containing rice grains within an inhabited area.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense when teaching the Dhamma to someone holding a sunshade:
an offense of wrong-doing.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by teaching the Dhamma to someone holding a staff:
an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by teaching the Dhamma to someone holding a weapon: an offense of wrong-doing.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by teaching the Dhamma to someone who has a weapon in hand:
an offense of wrong-doing.
The Sixth Chapter: On Whistling.
7.7. The Chapter on Sandals:
One commits one offense by teaching the Dhamma to someone wearing sandals out of disrespect.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by teaching the Dhamma to someone wearing sandals:
an offense of wrong-doing.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by teaching the Dhamma to someone traveling in a vehicle:
an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by teaching the Dhamma to someone lying on a bed: an offense of wrong-doing.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
By teaching the Dhamma to one sitting with his arms folded out of disrespect, one commits one offense:
an offense of wrong-doing.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by teaching the Dhamma to someone with their head wrapped;
it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by teaching the Dhamma to someone with their head covered; it is an offense of wrong-doing.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, while sitting on the ground, one commits one offense by teaching the Dhamma to someone sitting on a seat:
an offense of wrong-doing.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by teaching the Dhamma while seated on a low seat to one who is seated on a high seat:
an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by teaching the Dhamma while standing to one who is seated.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, one who walks behind while teaching the Dhamma to one walking ahead incurs one offense:
an offense of wrong-doing.
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by teaching the Dhamma while walking off the path to someone walking on the path:
an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by standing and voiding excrement or urine: an offense of wrong-doing.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, one commits one offense by voiding excrement, urine, or spittle on a green crop:
an offense of wrong-doing.
In dependence on disrespect, how many offenses does one incur by voiding feces, urine, or spittle in water?
In dependence on disrespect, one incurs one offense by voiding feces, urine, or spittle in water:
an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Out of disrespect, one commits this one offense by voiding excrement, urine, or spitting in water.
The seventh section, on sandals, is concluded.
The Sekhiya rules are finished.
The second section, on the completion of the offense, is finished.
